period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.textbook_anchor: So Many Kinds of Plants — Students write the names of trees they can recognise and recall where they have seen them, near home or on the way to school (p. 49)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 49 illustrations of trees (mango, coconut, banyan, peepal, etc.)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the opening story of three children walking to school from Textbook p. 49, pausing to invite children to share what plants they notice on their own walk to school. The discussion is kept concrete and personal — smells, shade, colours, textures they have experienced.

Teacher introduces trees as plants with one big woody trunk, deep roots, and many branches, using the textbook illustrations. Children examine the pictures of mango, coconut, khejri, jackfruit, banyan, amaltas, peepal, and chinar and share which they have seen and what they remember about each — its smell, the shade it gives, or the fruit it bears.

Students open Textbook p. 49 and write in their notebooks the names of trees they can recognise, noting where they have seen each one — near home, on the way to school, or in a park. Children who know a local or mother-tongue name for a tree are encouraged to write both names.

A few volunteers share their lists aloud. Teacher compiles a class list on the board, celebrating the variety. Teacher closes by asking children to look carefully at any tree they pass on their way home — its trunk, branches, and leaves — and be ready to describe what they notice.

periods.implied_lo: Students can recall and name plants from their immediate environment and describe where they have observed them.
periods.section_context: Trees: mango, coconut, khejri, jackfruit, banyan, amaltas, peepal, chinar; features: woody trunk, deep roots, many branches; sensory features: shade, smell, leaf colour and texture.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone hugged a tree trunk — was it smooth or rough? Did any tree near your home give you shade or fruit?' If children name local trees by regional names, affirm those names warmly alongside textbook names.

periods.activity_title: Sorting Shrubs — From Garden to Our Plate
periods.textbook_anchor: Shrubs — Students write the names of shrubs they have seen and identify them in the textbook pictures (p. 50)
materials: Fresh or dried tulsi leaves (if available)
A small sprig of curry leaf or rose (optional, whatever is locally available)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 50 pictures of hibiscus, rose, tulsi, curry leaf, and pulse plants

time_bands.activity: Teacher passes around any available shrub specimen (tulsi, curry leaf, or rose sprig) for children to touch and smell. Teacher asks: 'How is this plant different from a tree?' Children share observations and teacher builds the definition of a shrub — several woody stems, branches close to the ground, medium size — on the board.

Students open Textbook p. 50 and observe the pictures of hibiscus, rose, tulsi, curry leaf, and pulse shrubs. Teacher draws attention to the multiple stems visible at ground level in each picture. Students discuss which of these shrubs they have seen — in a garden, courtyard, temple, or kitchen — and what the plant was used for at home.

Students write in their notebooks: the names of shrubs they have seen and where; and the mother-tongue names they know for those shrubs. Teacher prompts the pulse connection: 'The toor dal, masoor, moong, and urad we eat — these are seeds from shrubs just like the ones on this page.' Students note this discovery alongside their shrub list.

Quick sharing: each child names one shrub from their list and says what it is used for — eaten, offered in prayer, used as medicine, grown in the garden. Teacher notes the variety of uses on the board and invites children to find out from a family member what other shrubs grow near their home.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe features that distinguish one plant category from another and connect familiar food plants to that category.
periods.section_context: Shrubs: hibiscus, rose, tulsi (holy basil), curry leaf; pulse shrubs: toor, masoor, moong, urad; features: several woody stems, branches close to ground, medium size; mother-tongue naming.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt children to recall dal dishes eaten at home and connect them to the shrub pictures on p. 50 — this surfaces culturally embedded plant knowledge naturally. Ask: 'Do you know what we call this plant at home — is the name different in your language?'

periods.activity_title: Soft Stems and Tall Grasses — Herbs We Know
periods.textbook_anchor: Herbs and Grasses — Students write the names of herbs they have seen and where they have seen them (p. 52)
materials: A small bunch of fresh mint or coriander (optional, from a local market or school garden)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 52 illustrations of herbs (mint, tomato, coriander, mustard) and grasses (paddy, wheat, bajra, bamboo, sugarcane)

time_bands.activity: Teacher holds up (or mimes crushing) a mint or coriander leaf and asks children to describe the smell. Teacher asks: 'Is this plant big like a tree or bushy like a shrub?' Children notice it is smaller and softer. Teacher introduces herbs as plants with soft stems that never become woody, and grasses as a special type of herb with thin, hollow stems.

Students look at Textbook p. 52 illustrations together. Teacher names each herb — mint, tomato, coriander, mustard — and asks children to say where they have seen it: in a pot on the balcony, in the kitchen garden, in a field, in the market. Teacher then moves to grasses and asks: 'Can you guess what food comes from paddy? From wheat? From bajra?' Children connect grains they eat to the grass plants pictured.

Students write in their notebooks the names of herbs they have seen and where, using Textbook p. 52 as a reference. Teacher encourages them to include herbs used in cooking at home. Children who know local names write them alongside the textbook names.

Class discussion: Teacher draws a simple comparison on the board — tree (one big woody trunk), shrub (several woody stems), herb (soft stem). Children use this to check their own plant examples from earlier units' content. Teacher asks: 'If sugarcane and bamboo are tall grasses, what does that tell us about how big a grass can get?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify plants into categories based on stem type and describe connections between familiar food grains and their plant source.
periods.section_context: Herbs: mint, tomato, coriander, mustard; grasses: paddy, wheat, bajra, jowar, ragi, sugarcane, bamboo; features: soft stem (herbs), thin flat hollow-stemmed leaves (grasses); staple food grain connection.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Draw out the food-grain connection gently: ask which grains the children ate and let them discover that the grain is a grass seed. If children name local varieties of rice or millet, celebrate those names as equally valid.

periods.activity_title: Spotting Climbers and Creepers — A Schoolyard Hunt
periods.textbook_anchor: Climbers and Creepers — Students stand in groups near a tree or shrub and count how many kinds of plants they can spot (p. 54)
materials: Clipboards or hard books to write on outdoors
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 53–54 pictures of climbers (money plant, jasmine, bottle gourd) and creepers (watermelon, pumpkin)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces climbers and creepers using Textbook p. 53–54 pictures. Key distinction is built through questions: 'Does this plant hold onto a wall or another plant to go up? That is a climber. Does it spread along the ground? That is a creeper.' Children name examples they already know — jasmine on a fence, pumpkin in a garden.

Teacher explains the outdoor group task: in groups of two to four, children will stand near any tree or shrub in or near the school and look in all directions — including down near their feet — to spot and record as many plant types as possible. Groups are formed and notebooks are readied.

Groups go outdoors and carry out the observation from Textbook p. 54. Each group records what they spot — trees, shrubs, herbs, grasses, climbers, creepers — naming plants where they can and noting which category each belongs to. Teacher circulates, prompting: 'Look along the wall — do you see anything climbing? Look at the ground near the roots — any plant spreading along the soil?'

Back in class, each group shares their findings. Teacher builds a combined class tally on the board. Children also write the local-language names they know for any climbers or creepers spotted, completing the written task from Textbook p. 54. Teacher asks: 'Which plant type was easiest to spot near our school? Which was hardest to find?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can distinguish climbers from creepers using observable stem and growth features, and conduct a structured outdoor plant-spotting inquiry.
periods.section_context: Climbers: money plant, jasmine, bottle gourd; creepers: watermelon, pumpkin; classification of marigold, neem, jujube by type; local-language naming; schoolyard plant-count activity.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ensure groups look both up (along walls and fences) and down (near the ground) — children tend to look only at eye level. Ask: 'Does this plant hold on with its stem, or does it just rest along the ground?' to sharpen the climber/creeper distinction.

periods.activity_title: Making Friends with a Plant — First Observation
periods.textbook_anchor: Parts of a Plant — Students choose a plant, name it, and record their first close observation of its leaves, flowers, and fruits in a table (p. 55)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 55 labelled diagram of a tomato plant showing roots, stem, leaves, flowers, fruits, and seeds

time_bands.activity: Teacher points to the labelled tomato plant diagram on Textbook p. 55 and names each part — roots, stem, leaves, flowers, fruits, seeds — inviting children to point to the same part on any plant visible through the classroom window or in a pot. Teacher asks: 'Which part do we eat in a tomato? In a mango? In spinach?'

Teacher introduces the 'make friends with a plant' idea from Textbook p. 55: each child will choose one plant — a shrub or tree in or near the school — give it a name, and observe it closely today. The observation will be recorded in the table format shown in the textbook: leaves (many/few/none), flowers (many/few/none), fruits (many/few/none).

Children go to their chosen plant and spend an unhurried period observing it. They record their observations in their notebooks using the table format from Textbook p. 55, noting whether there are many, a few, or no leaves, flowers, and fruits. Teacher circulates and encourages children to also note the colour of leaves, whether any fruits are forming, and what the stem feels like.

Back in class, children share what they chose and one detail they noticed that surprised them. Teacher introduces the idea that they can revisit this same plant over time to notice how it changes — whether new leaves appear, flowers open, or fruits develop. Children write the name they gave their plant in their notebooks.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify and name the parts of a plant through direct observation and record what they see using a structured table.
periods.section_context: Parts of a plant: roots, stem, leaves, flowers, fruits, seeds; tomato plant labelled diagram; leaves of peepal, mango, lotus, khejri; first observation of chosen plant's leaves, flowers, and fruits.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Let children choose their own plant — ownership deepens the observation. Ask: 'Why did you choose this plant? What was the first thing you noticed about it?' If a child picks a grass or herb, affirm that these also have all the parts shown in the diagram.

periods.activity_title: Leaves Up Close — Draw, Label, Describe
periods.textbook_anchor: Parts of a Plant — Students observe leaves, then draw, colour, and label them and describe their features to a classmate (p. 57)
materials: Two or three different leaves collected from the schoolyard (one per child or pair)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 57 illustrations of varied leaves; board diagram showing leaf descriptors (colour, shape, size, texture, smell)

time_bands.activity: Each child or pair receives one or two leaves collected from the schoolyard. Teacher asks children to hold the leaf up to the light, run a finger along its edge, and press it gently to check texture. Five descriptors are written on the board: colour, shape, size, texture, smell. Children share first impressions aloud.

Students open Textbook p. 57 and follow the activity: they draw their leaf carefully in their notebook, colour it to match, and label it with the plant name if known. They then add descriptive words for each of the five features beside the drawing. Teacher circulates, encouraging careful observation of vein patterns and edge shapes.

Children describe their leaf to a partner using only words — no showing the leaf — while the partner draws what they hear. Then they compare the drawn version to the real leaf. The class discusses: which features were easiest to describe? Which made the partner's drawing most accurate?

Brief whole-class reflection: 'What statements can we make about leaves after doing this activity?' Teacher collects three or four statements on the board — e.g. 'Leaves of the same plant can look different' or 'Some leaves smell stronger than others' — and asks children to write their own statement in their notebooks.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present observations of natural objects through drawing, labelling, and oral description using multiple sensory features.
periods.section_context: Leaf observation and drawing activity; descriptors: colour, shape, size, texture, smell; leaves from schoolyard; partner description-and-drawing exchange; class statements about leaves.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Encourage children to notice vein patterns and leaf edges — these are distinctive and often overlooked. Ask pairs: 'Which word made your partner's drawing most accurate — was it the shape word or the colour word?'

periods.activity_title: Blindfold Fruit Smell and Bark Rubbing
periods.textbook_anchor: Parts of a Plant — Students blindfold themselves and identify fruits by smell, then do bark rubbing and try to identify trees by bark pattern (p. 57, p. 59)
materials: Two or three different fruits (whole and cut pieces — e.g. banana, guava, orange, or whatever is locally available)

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets up two inquiry stations: one with whole and cut fruit pieces covered by a cloth, one with sheets of paper and crayons for bark rubbing. Teacher explains both activities briefly so children know what is coming.

In pairs, children carry out the blindfold smell activity from Textbook p. 57: one child is blindfolded while the partner gradually brings a whole fruit closer; the blindfolded child says when they can smell it and names the fruit. They repeat with a cut piece of the same fruit and notice whether cut fruit is easier to smell from farther away. Pairs swap roles and try a different fruit.

Children take their paper and crayon to a tree trunk in or adjacent to the classroom and carry out the bark rubbing from Textbook p. 59: they press paper against the bark, rub the crayon across it gently, and observe the pattern that appears. They write the tree name or a description on the reverse. All rubbings are collected and displayed; children try to match rubbings to trees.

Quick debrief: Which fruit could be smelled from farthest away? Was cut fruit easier to identify than whole fruit? Which bark patterns were most distinctive? Teacher asks children to note their findings as two sentences in their notebook.

periods.implied_lo: Students can perform a simple sensory inquiry, record findings, and draw conclusions about how observable features vary across natural objects.
periods.section_context: Blindfold fruit smell experiment: whole and cut fruit pieces; bark rubbing activity: bark patterns of available school trees; comparison of whole vs. cut fruit smell distance.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Use fruits that are familiar and locally common — the investigation should feel connected to everyday experience. Ask: 'Why do you think cut fruit smells stronger?' to prompt reasoning rather than just recall.

periods.activity_title: Reflect, Write, and Make Leaf Rangoli
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students collect fallen leaves and flowers and arrange them in patterns to make a rangoli or create animal shapes (p. 61)
materials: Fallen leaves and flowers collected from the schoolyard (students collect at the start)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 60–61 reflection prompts and rangoli activity illustration

time_bands.activity: Children spend a brief, unhurried time outside gathering fallen leaves and flowers from the schoolyard — no plucking from living plants. Back in class, they arrange their collection on their desk and spend a moment looking at the variety of shapes, sizes, and colours they have gathered.

Teacher leads a discussion using the reflection prompts from Textbook p. 60: 'What would happen if there were no plants?' and 'How do roots and stems help a plant grow?' Children contribute ideas and teacher notes key points on the board. Students then write in their notebooks: a list of plants they have seen near school or home, identifying each as tree, shrub, herb, grass, climber, or creeper; and which part of the plant helped them identify its type.

Students create their rangoli on a flat surface (desk or floor) using the fallen leaves and flowers they collected, following the activity from Textbook p. 61. They may make a repeating pattern or arrange leaves into an animal shape. Teacher encourages them to notice how the same leaf placed differently makes a new pattern — just as rangoli artists do.

Gallery walk: children move around briefly to see each other's leaf rangoli. Each child then writes two sentences in their notebook describing their favourite plant and why it is their favourite. Teacher closes by asking: 'If a friend who had never seen a plant asked you to describe one, which part of the plant would you start with, and why?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can express understanding of plant diversity and plant importance through written classification, discussion, and a nature-based creative arrangement.
periods.section_context: Discussion: importance of plants, role of roots and stems; written classification of local plants by type; identifying plant part used for classification; favourite plant description; leaf-and-flower rangoli and animal shapes activity.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Let children use the local names they know for plants in their written list — all names are equally valid. Ask: 'Have you seen rangoli made with flowers or leaves at home or during a festival?' to connect the creative activity to living traditions.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya sees a plant on her way to school. It has one big, thick, woody trunk with deep roots and many branches spreading out above. Which type of plant is this most likely to be?
assessment_items.annotation: Accept 'tree' only. The question targets the defining feature of a tree — one big woody trunk with deep roots — as introduced in this section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can recall and name plants from their immediate environment and describe where they have observed them.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'shrub' indicates the student has not yet distinguished between one big trunk (tree) and several woody stems close to the ground (shrub).
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'climber' indicates the student has confused upright, self-supporting growth with the flexible stems of climbing plants.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'herb' indicates the student has not connected stem woodiness and size as distinguishing features; they may be recalling only that herbs are small without noting the trunk feature.

assessment_items.question_text: Rajan says that the toor dal he eats at home comes from a shrub. His friend says that cannot be true because shrubs are only garden plants. Who is correct, and how would you explain it?
expected_elements: Rajan is correct.
Toor (and masoor, moong, or urad) are pulses whose seeds come from shrub plants.
A shrub is a medium-sized plant with several woody stems growing close to the ground — it is not only a garden plant.
Shrubs can be useful food plants, not just decorative ones.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for identifying Rajan as correct and explaining that pulses are seeds of shrubs. Partial credit if the student correctly names Rajan but gives no explanation. Regional variation note: students may name locally common pulses such as chana or kulthi in addition to or instead of toor, masoor, moong, urad — all are acceptable.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe features that distinguish one plant category from another and connect familiar food plants to that category.

competency.competency_text: Describes usage of natural resources in their immediate environment

expected_elements: Rajan is correct.
Toor (and masoor, moong, or urad) are pulses whose seeds come from shrub plants.
A shrub is a medium-sized plant with several woody stems growing close to the ground — it is not only a garden plant.
Shrubs can be useful food plants, not just decorative ones.

assessment_items.question_text: Asha wants to find an herb in her school garden. She should look for a plant that has —

options.label: A
options.text: A flexible stem that winds around other plants

options.label: B
options.text: A soft stem that does not become woody

options.label: D
options.text: Several woody stems growing close to the ground

assessment_items.annotation: Accept 'C' only. The defining feature of an herb — soft stem that does not become woody — is the correct answer.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify plants into categories based on stem type and describe connections between familiar food grains and their plant source.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes diversity among plants, and birds and animals in their immediate environment (shape, sounds, food habits, growth, habitat)

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'one big thick woody trunk' indicates the student is recalling the tree definition rather than the herb definition — a confusion between the two ends of the size scale.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'several woody stems close to the ground' indicates the student is recalling the shrub definition; they have not yet separated shrub from herb by stem texture.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'flexible stem that winds around other plants' indicates the student is confusing herbs with climbers — a mix-up of two categories of smaller plants.

assessment_items.question_text: During the schoolyard plant hunt, Meena's group saw a plant spreading along the ground with large leaves, and another plant growing up a fence by winding its stem around the wire. Name the type each plant belongs to and give one feature that helped your group decide.
expected_elements: The plant spreading along the ground is a creeper.
The plant growing up the fence by winding its stem is a climber.
One observable feature for the creeper: its stem spreads along the ground / it does not climb upward.
One observable feature for the climber: it uses its stem (or tendrils) to hold onto a support and grows upward.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for correctly naming both types and providing a valid feature for each. Partial credit if both names are correct but no feature is stated, or if one name and one feature are correct. Students may name locally observed climbers or creepers as examples — accept any valid local plant name.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can distinguish climbers from creepers using observable stem and growth features, and conduct a structured outdoor plant-spotting inquiry.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: The plant spreading along the ground is a creeper.
The plant growing up the fence by winding its stem is a climber.
One observable feature for the creeper: its stem spreads along the ground / it does not climb upward.
One observable feature for the climber: it uses its stem (or tendrils) to hold onto a support and grows upward.

assessment_items.question_text: Kavya chose a tomato plant as her 'plant friend'. She wants to draw a table to record what she saw. Which set of plant parts should she include in her table?
assessment_items.annotation: Accept 'B' only. The textbook's observation table for the plant-friend activity specifically records leaves, flowers, and fruits.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and name the parts of a plant through direct observation and record what they see using a structured table.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'roots, bark, thorns, and seeds' indicates the student is recalling plant-related vocabulary without connecting it to the specific observation table structure for the plant-friend activity.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'colour, smell, and shadow' indicates the student is confusing sensory descriptors used in the leaf and fruit activities with the parts-of-plant observation framework.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'trunk, branches, and soil' indicates the student is mixing environmental context with plant-part vocabulary, or recalling tree features rather than the observation task.

assessment_items.task: Pick up one leaf from the ground near you. Look at it carefully. In your notebook, draw the leaf as accurately as you can. Colour it to match the real leaf. Write three describing words beside your drawing — one for its colour, one for its shape, and one for its texture (how it feels). Then write one sentence: 'After looking at this leaf, I noticed that ___.'
assessment_items.scaffold:
My leaf drawing: [space to draw and colour]
Colour word: ___
Shape word: ___
Texture word: ___
After looking at this leaf, I noticed that ___.
format_of_output: A labelled, coloured drawing of the leaf
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any leaf from the local environment. Drawings need not be artistically perfect — assess accuracy of observable features (vein direction, edge shape, colour match). Descriptive words should correspond to the leaf in hand, not to a generic leaf. The observation sentence should reflect something the child actually noticed — there is no single correct answer.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present observations of natural objects through drawing, labelling, and oral description using multiple sensory features.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can move from direct sensory observation to a multi-modal presentation — combining visual (drawing), linguistic (descriptor words), and reflective (sentence) outputs for the same natural object.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold separates three distinct skills — drawing accuracy, vocabulary precision, and personal observation — so the teacher can see which a child has and which needs support. A child who draws well but writes vague descriptors needs vocabulary support; a child with vivid words but a schematic drawing needs observation scaffolding.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: drawing shows distinctive leaf features (vein pattern, edge shape); colour is matched to the real leaf; descriptive words are specific (e.g. 'spiky edges', 'dark green', 'rough'); observation sentence is grounded in something actually noticed. Weak: drawing is a generic oval; descriptors are interchangeable (e.g. 'green', 'nice', 'soft'); observation sentence is a copied fact rather than a personal noticing.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who find drawing difficult may trace the leaf outline first and then add details. Children who struggle to write may dictate their three words and sentence to the teacher or a peer scribe. Children who cannot hold a crayon steadily may do a leaf rubbing as the drawing component.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Labelled drawing with written descriptors and one reflective sentence
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The leaf-observation activity in this unit explicitly asks children to draw, colour, label, and describe — the task format mirrors the activity so the assessment is a natural continuation of the learning experience.

assessment_items.question_text: In the fruit-smell experiment, Vikram found that he could smell a cut piece of guava from much farther away than the whole guava. Give one reason why this might be so, and name one other fruit that you think would have a strong smell.
expected_elements: When a fruit is cut, more of its surface is exposed, releasing more smell into the air — making it easier to detect from farther away.
A named fruit that the student thinks has a strong smell (any locally familiar fruit is acceptable — e.g. mango, jackfruit, banana, orange, pineapple).
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for a plausible reason involving increased surface/exposed area and any named fruit. Partial credit if only the fruit name is given with no reason. Regional variation note: accept any fruit familiar in the student's region — there is no single correct fruit answer.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can perform a simple sensory inquiry, record findings, and draw conclusions about how observable features vary across natural objects.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: When a fruit is cut, more of its surface is exposed, releasing more smell into the air — making it easier to detect from farther away.
A named fruit that the student thinks has a strong smell (any locally familiar fruit is acceptable — e.g. mango, jackfruit, banana, orange, pineapple).

assessment_items.task: Look around the area near your school or home. Think of five plants you have seen there. In your notebook, make a table with two columns: 'Plant name' and 'Type of plant'. Fill in your five plants and write what type each one is — tree, shrub, herb, grass, climber, or creeper. Then write one sentence about why plants are important to you.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My plant table:
| Plant name | Type of plant |
|---|---|
| 1. | |
| 2. | |
| 3. | |
| 4. | |
| 5. | |

Plants are important to me because ___.
format_of_output: A two-column table with five plant names and their types
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any five plants known to the student, including local and regional names. Classification should correspond to the features discussed in the chapter — evaluate the reasoning, not just the answer. The importance sentence may reflect any dimension (food, shade, beauty, air, materials) — there is no single correct answer. Regional variation note: local plant names in any language are fully acceptable.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express understanding of plant diversity and plant importance through written classification, discussion, and a nature-based creative arrangement.

competency.competency_text: Describes usage of natural resources in their immediate environment

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The child can apply the classification framework built across the chapter to plants from their own environment, and articulate why plants matter — connecting natural-world knowledge to personal significance.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The table format separates naming from classifying, so the teacher can see whether a child knows plants but struggles to classify them, or classifies correctly but uses only textbook examples rather than local ones. The final sentence reveals whether the child has internalised any reason for plant importance.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: five distinct plants are named, including at least one local or regional plant; types are correctly assigned with no obvious mismatches (e.g. a tree labelled 'herb'); importance sentence is specific and personal (e.g. 'We eat rice from a grass plant'). Weak: fewer than five plants or repeated examples; types are guessed without regard to features; importance sentence is a copied phrase ('plants give us oxygen') with no personal connection.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who struggle to write plant names may draw the plant and label it with a local name or description. Children who cannot write may dictate entries to a peer or the teacher. The table may be filled in mother-tongue names — transliteration is fully acceptable.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification table plus one reflective sentence
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The reflect section's write tasks explicitly ask children to list and classify local plants and describe their importance — the assessment task is a direct, compact version of that activity, giving all children an equal opportunity to draw on their own environment.
